purpose: The ways a running go program can HOLD layer-1 content. Not layer 1 (the data is fixed), not layer 3 (no operations beyond load-and-read-back), not the type system.
reference: language knowledge, checked against ../type_vocabulary/raw/go.types.json as a candidate checklist only (superseded node; not a decision instrument).

nothing.note: the nil value of an interface holding no type and no value.
a pointer typed to a whole number that happens to hold no address; the type persists even though the pointee is absent.

truth.note: two values, no numeric side in the source spelling.

whole.note: signed 32-bit; the narrow end, silently wraps values that do not fit.
unsigned 64-bit; reaches u64 max, refuses anything below zero.
the platform-width whole number; 64-bit on every mainstream go target today, so it tracks int64 in practice.

fractional.note: IEEE double, the ordinary fractional holder.
IEEE single; holds every base value at lower precision.

text.note: an immutable byte sequence taken as utf-8, the ordinary text holder.
holds text only as raw bytes; the codepoints are gone until decoded.
one array element per codepoint rather than per byte.

sequence.note: growable ordered run backed by an array, one declared element kind.
fixed length baked into the type; unlike c a zero-length array is legal.
each position boxes its own type; the go sequence holder that takes the mixed row.
a doubly linked run of boxed elements; insertion anywhere is cheap, indexing is not.
sequence.read: func() string { s := "["; first := true; for e := v.Front(); e != nil; e = e.Next() { if !first { s += "," }; s += fmt.Sprintf("%v", e.Value); first = false }; return s + "]" }()

probes.mixed:
v := list.New()
v.PushBack(int64(1))
v.PushBack("two")
v.PushBack(3.0)
v.PushBack(true)
v.PushBack(nil)

keyed.note: name to element, no order kept; read back sorts keys to make the probe reproducible.
keyed.read: func() string { ks := make([]string, 0, len(v)); for k := range v { ks = append(ks, k) }; sort.Strings(ks); s := ""; first := true; for _, k := range ks { if !first { s += "," }; s += fmt.Sprintf("%s=%v", k, v[k]); first = false }; return s }()

keyed.spelling: type R struct{ A int64 }; R{A: 1}
keyed.note: field names are fixed when the shape is written, not when the data arrives; the odd keys are not spellable as field names at all.

probes.flat:
type R3 struct{ A, B, C int64 }
v := R3{A: 1, B: 2, C: 3}
probes.intlike:
type RI struct{ 1 int64; B int64 }
v := RI{1: 1, B: 2}
probes.emptykey:
type RE struct{ "" string }
v := RE{}
probes.nested:
type RN struct{ Outer []int64 }
v := RN{Outer: []int64{1, 2}}

nesting.note: nesting by repeating the same holder; go's %v formatter walks nested slices and maps on its own, no hand-written printer needed.
interface{} composed ad hoc; the one go holder here that takes every layer-1 form in one element position without a shape declared ahead of time, which is what mixed-depth nesting needs.

identity.note: a slice header copies but its backing array can still alias; here cap equals len so the mutating append reallocates and the second position stays untouched, reading as copied. Self-containment by value degrades to a harmless copy rather than a compile refusal.
the natural go reference; two positions holding the same pointer name one object, and mutation through either is visible through both.
the idiomatic go graph-building shape: a collection holds pointers to heap-allocated nodes, so sharing and cycles are ordinary pointer aliasing.
